idiom_name: HashMap<Key, Memo> on the parser struct, entry cloned before the recursive call
implementation_notes: The memo is a HashMap<(RuleId, usize), Memo> owned by the parser, with Memo an enum (Ok { node: NodeId, next: usize } | Fail) so a cached failure is a value and Option's 'missing' never has to double as 'failed'. The borrow checker dictates the shape of the rule wrapper: get() returns a reference into the map, so the hit must be cloned or copied out before the recursive call that needs &mut self again; holding the reference across the recursion does not compile, and wrapping the map in a RefCell trades that compile error for a runtime 'already borrowed' panic (the docs state borrow_mut panics while a borrow is active). What replaces the classic memo-table object is that the table is a field, the rules are methods, and one rule() wrapper performs lookup/store with a derived Hash/Eq key; HashMap's docs also pin the invariants - Eq and Hash must agree, and a key whose hash or equality changes while stored is a logic error.
pitfalls: Holding the get() reference across the recursive rule call is a borrow error; the RefCell workaround compiles but panics at runtime when borrows overlap, so clone the entry out or split the borrow.
HashMap requires Eq + Hash to agree and treats a stored key whose hash or equality changes as a logic error: never key the memo on a type with interior mutability.
The default RandomState hasher (SipHash) is slower than needed for small integer keys; a cheaper BuildHasher or the dense-table variant is the usual fix.

variants.name: Flat Vec<Memo> indexed by rule and position with arena NodeIds
variants.idiom_name: flat Vec<Memo> (rules x (len + 1)) with a three-state enum, nodes in an arena
variants.implementation_notes: Positions are bounded by the input length, so the table can be a single Vec<Memo> of rules * (len + 1) cells addressed arithmetically, with a three-state Memo (Unknown | Ok { node, next } | Fail) so 'not computed' and 'failed' are distinct without a nested Option. Nodes live in an arena (Vec<Node> returning NodeId), which removes lifetimes from the memo entirely and keeps cached entries Copy - the reason this layout is common in Rust parser code. The trade is allocation shape: the table is allocated up front for every rule even where most rules are never attempted at most positions (Ford's per-category split is the escape), and the flat index must be computed in usize to avoid silent overflow.
pitfalls: The dense table costs rules x (len + 1) cells up front and can exceed the hash-map version for grammars with many rules that are never tried at most positions.
The parser owns both arena and memo, so a rule body must not hold &Node across a call that pushes into the arena (the Vec may reallocate): exchange NodeIds, not references.
Index arithmetic in a narrower integer type overflows for large inputs - compute rule * cols + pos in usize and size the vector from the actual input.
